scenarios.title: Name the metric before you build the thing
scenarios.what: shipped an LLM query assistant in ~1 month for about $30/month in API cost — and found the real failure was discoverability, not the model
scenarios.situation: You have one afternoon and a free-tier API key. Before you write any code, your lead asks a single question: how will you know next week whether this helped anyone?
scenarios.given: A 5,000-row SQLite dataset, a free-tier LLM key, and a one-page product brief with no metrics in it.
done: A natural-language-to-query feature that answers 10 sample questions
An activation metric defined and written down BEFORE the feature was built
Instrumentation that records it, and a measured baseline from the no-feature path
scenarios.verify: Harness asserts the metric definition file predates the first feature commit (git timestamps), and that the events table contains both cohorts.
scenarios.matters: Honeycomb's feature worked and still under-performed on the free tier — because users never noticed it. No model change fixes that, and only the metric revealed it.

scenarios.title: The answer that contradicted the policy page
scenarios.what: a support chatbot told a grieving passenger he could claim a bereavement fare retroactively; the airline's own published policy said the opposite, and a tribunal held the airline liable
scenarios.situation: You are handed a 20-page policy corpus and a chatbot that answers from it. Somewhere in that corpus two policies contradict each other. Find the question that makes the bot give a confidently wrong answer.
scenarios.given: A 20-document policy corpus containing several deliberate near-miss clauses, and a working ungrounded chatbot.
done: At least three questions that produce a confidently wrong answer
For each, the authoritative clause the answer contradicts, cited by page
A one-paragraph note on which of the three would have cost real money
scenarios.verify: Hidden test replays your questions against a grounded reference implementation and asserts the answers genuinely diverge.
scenarios.matters: Air Canada argued the chatbot was a separate entity responsible for its own statements. The tribunal disagreed. Anything your system says, you said.

scenarios.title: The five-stage cascade and where it loses accuracy
scenarios.what: a WhatsApp bot chaining ASR → translation → LLM retrieval → translation → TTS to answer Indian-language questions about government schemes; no per-stage error budget was ever published
scenarios.situation: You are rebuilding Jugalbandi at laptop scale: a citizen asks in Hindi or Telugu by voice, and gets an answer about a welfare scheme. Five models in a chain. Your job is not to build it — it is to find out which stage is losing you the most accuracy.
scenarios.given: 20 scheme PDFs, 50 hand-written Hindi/Telugu queries with gold answers, faster-whisper tiny, a distilled translation checkpoint, a free-tier LLM, a free TTS.
done: The full five-stage cascade running end to end
Per-stage accuracy measured independently, not just end to end
A written error budget showing where the compounding actually happens
A recommendation on which single stage to fix first, with the number to justify it
scenarios.verify: `make eval` scores each stage against its own gold set and asserts the end-to-end number is reconcilable with the per-stage numbers.
scenarios.matters: Microsoft's own write-up concedes the models make mistakes and covers only 171 of roughly 20,000 schemes. Nobody published where in the chain the errors come from. You will.

scenarios.title: The rows that were never there
scenarios.what: roughly 16,000 COVID-19 cases went unreported because results were held in a legacy spreadsheet format that silently stops at a fixed row limit
scenarios.situation: Your ingestion job reports success. Downstream counts are wrong and nobody can say why. The loader hit a hard limit and did not raise.
scenarios.given: A loader that reads three files, one of which exceeds a format limit, and a downstream count that looks plausible.
done: The truncation found and its exact cause named
A row-count reconciliation check that fails loudly on the same input
Proof the check catches it before anything downstream runs
scenarios.verify: Hidden test swaps in a differently-sized file and asserts your check still fires.
scenarios.matters: Nobody at PHE wrote a bad model. A file format quietly ate the data and every dashboard downstream looked fine.

scenarios.title: 95% per word, 44% per document
scenarios.what: mid-90s single-word OCR accuracy produced only about 44% document-level exact match, because of merged words, fragmented words and spurious boxes
scenarios.situation: You are given an OCR system that scores 95% on individual words. Your manager wants to ship it. Measure what it actually does to a whole document.
scenarios.given: 200 word-crop images with labels, 30 full documents with ground truth, and a working word-level recogniser.
done: Word-level accuracy and document-level exact match both measured
The gap explained by failure class (merged / fragmented / spurious)
A one-page recommendation on which failure class to fix first
scenarios.verify: Harness recomputes both metrics from your outputs and asserts you reported the document-level number, not just the word-level one.
scenarios.matters: Dropbox shipped only after building confidence thresholds, dictionary validation and a word-reassembly stage. The 95% number was true and useless.

scenarios.title: Header fields are easy. Line items are where it dies.
scenarios.what: a fine-tuned T5 exceeded 90% on invoice header fields but collapsed on line items, with a considerable accuracy drop from the second line onward — and fine-tuning actively induced hallucinations
scenarios.situation: Extract structured data from 40 invoices. Report one accuracy number and your reviewer will accept it. Report two and you will find out the system does not work.
scenarios.given: 40 invoice PDFs across 4 templates, a JSON target schema with header and line-item sections, a free-tier LLM.
done: Extraction to the fixed schema
Header-field accuracy and line-item accuracy reported separately
Line-item accuracy broken down by line position (1st, 2nd, 3rd…)
scenarios.verify: Hidden test asserts your report contains a per-position line-item breakdown and that it matches recomputed values.
scenarios.matters: Uber tried rules, then RPA, then fine-tuned open models — and still ended up with a mandatory human review stage because line items would not hold.

scenarios.title: Two hundred jobs at the top of the hour
scenarios.what: over 10,000 DAGs and 150,000 task runs a day; jobs clustered on identical cron schedules until randomised, hash-seeded scheduling smoothed the load
scenarios.situation: Your scheduler has 200 jobs. Half of them are on `0 * * * *`. Everything is slow on the hour and idle the rest of the time.
scenarios.given: A local Airflow with a LocalExecutor and 200 generated DAGs, half on the same cron.
done: The stall reproduced and measured
A hash-seeded randomised schedule applied
A before/after histogram of task starts across the hour
scenarios.verify: Harness parses your DAG definitions and asserts start times are deterministic per DAG but distributed across the window.
scenarios.matters: Shopify's fix is four lines of hashing. Finding that it was the problem took production degradation nobody could see in the DAG code.

scenarios.title: It can read the language. It cannot see the script.
scenarios.what: LoRA fine-tuning fixed Latin scripts but still failed on Thai and Vietnamese — the diagnosis was that the vision encoder had almost no SEA-script data, while the text decoder knew the languages fine
scenarios.situation: A multimodal model reads your English documents perfectly and mangles the Devanagari ones. Everyone on your team assumes the model does not know Hindi. Prove them wrong.
scenarios.given: The same 30 sentences rendered as images in Latin, Devanagari and Tamil scripts, plus the same sentences as plain text.
done: Accuracy measured on image input vs text input for each script
Evidence isolating whether the failure is in reading or in understanding
A one-paragraph conclusion naming which component is at fault
scenarios.verify: Hidden test checks you ran both the image and text arms and that your conclusion matches your own numbers.
scenarios.matters: Grab spent four rejected approaches before locating the fault. The diagnosis — text-fluent, visually blind — is invisible unless you ablate.

scenarios.title: The cheaper model that cost more
scenarios.what: swapping in a cheaper LLM cut cost as expected, and the same post reports a 60% accuracy drop on difficult attributes
scenarios.situation: Finance wants the model bill down. You have a cheaper model available and a benchmark that says it is nearly as good. The benchmark is averaged.
scenarios.given: 500 product records with attribute labels, split into easy and hard subsets you are not told about, two model options.
done: Both models measured on cost and on accuracy
Accuracy reported split by difficulty, not averaged
A recommendation with the trade stated in both directions
scenarios.verify: Harness asserts your report contains a difficulty-stratified breakdown and that the cost saving is quoted against the accuracy loss.
scenarios.matters: The cost win was real. So was the 60% drop hiding underneath the average. Both are in the same blog post.

scenarios.title: Rebuild it from nothing
scenarios.what: TextSense was designed so new document types onboard through configuration rather than new code — reproducibility was the design constraint
scenarios.situation: Your index was built three weeks ago by someone who has left. Rebuild it from the raw files and get byte-identical output. If you cannot, you do not have a pipeline — you have a folder.
scenarios.given: A raw document folder, an existing built index, and a broken half-documented build script.
done: `make index` rebuilds from raw inputs with no manual steps
Output is deterministic across two runs
A checksum manifest committed alongside
scenarios.verify: Harness runs `make index` twice from a clean clone and diffs the artefacts.
scenarios.matters: Every case in this catalogue that recovered from a data incident could rebuild. The ones that could not had to retrain from scratch.

scenarios.title: Rebuild the words
scenarios.what: the fix for the 44% document accuracy was CTC confidence scoring with three-tier filtering plus a 'Wordinator' that resolved merged and fragmented word boxes
scenarios.situation: You have the 95%-per-word recogniser from U2-M02 and a document accuracy in the forties. Build the layer that closes the gap.
scenarios.given: The recogniser, 30 documents with ground truth, a word list for validation.
done: Confidence-based three-tier filtering (accept / reject / validate against lexicon)
A word-reassembly stage handling merged and fragmented boxes
Document-level exact match improved, with the number before and after
A per-failure-class breakdown showing which fix bought what
scenarios.verify: `make eval` recomputes document accuracy; hidden documents test generalisation beyond the visible 30.
scenarios.matters: This layer, not the neural net, is what made Dropbox's OCR shippable. It is also the part nobody puts in a tutorial.

scenarios.title: Invoices that fight back
scenarios.what: rule-based systems and RPA were tried first and failed on new vendor formats; fine-tuned open models read the page but could not map onto Uber's data patterns
scenarios.situation: Fifty supplier invoices across four templates, plus a handful of skewed phone photos. Extract 15 header attributes and every line item into a fixed schema.
scenarios.given: 50 PDFs (mixed born-digital and scanned), a JSON schema, pdfplumber, Tesseract, a free-tier LLM.
done: Born-digital and scanned paths both working, with routing between them
Per-field accuracy for headers, per-position accuracy for line items
A human-review queue that routes exactly the fields below your confidence threshold
Cost per document measured
scenarios.verify: Hidden invoices in unseen templates test generalisation; harness asserts the review queue routes by measured confidence, not by a hardcoded list.
scenarios.matters: Uber's system reached ~90% overall and still shipped with mandatory human review. Knowing what to send a human is the engineering.

scenarios.title: Whose job is this?
scenarios.what: with DAGs deployed from many repos and generated dynamically, nobody could tell which team owned a failing job; accumulated metadata also slowed the UI and made upgrades take hours
scenarios.situation: A job has been failing for eleven days. The dashboard is red. No one has fixed it because no one knows whose it is.
scenarios.given: A local Airflow with 200 DAGs from three simulated repos, no ownership metadata, and a bloated metadata database.
done: An enforced ownership manifest that fails CI when a DAG has no owner
A metadata retention job, with the trade-off it costs you documented
Measured UI response time before and after retention
scenarios.verify: Harness adds an unowned DAG and asserts CI rejects it; measures metadata table sizes before and after.
scenarios.matters: Shopify's retention fix cost them the ability to run long backfills. Every operational fix buys something and sells something.

scenarios.title: Ingest sixty documents nobody has cleaned
scenarios.what: all three cases converge on the same finding: the parsing layer, not the model, decides the ceiling of everything downstream
scenarios.situation: Sixty real documents. Some are born-digital, some are phone photos, some are scanned at an angle, some are in a script your parser has never seen. Ship a pipeline that turns them into searchable, structured, version-stamped records — and a quality report that tells the truth about what failed.
scenarios.given: 60 mixed-quality documents, a target schema, and no guidance on which files are the awkward ones.
done: Deterministic `make index` from raw files
Routing between text-layer, OCR and multimodal paths based on measured signal
Every record carries source, page, document version and extraction confidence
A quality report naming which documents failed and why, by class
Per-document cost and wall-clock measured
A runbook a non-author can follow to add a new document
scenarios.verify: Hidden document set of 15 unseen files; harness asserts the quality report classifies each failure and that the confidence field correlates with actual correctness.
scenarios.matters: This is the single highest-leverage artifact in the whole curriculum. Every RAG scenario later in U9 stands on it, and every one of them fails if this is weak.

scenarios.title: A 40% business decline that never happened
scenarios.what: in October 2018 a silent data defect made reported job views drop 40–60%; it took 5 engineers 8 days to root-cause and 11 more to fix
scenarios.situation: Job views are down 47% week on week. The executive team wants to know what happened to the business. You suspect the business is fine.
scenarios.given: A 10,000-row events table with a segment whose tracking field starts returning null on a specific date.
done: The defect located and the affected segment named
Evidence distinguishing a data defect from a real decline
The check that would have caught it on day one
scenarios.verify: Harness re-injects the defect on a different date and segment and asserts your check fires within one day of onset.
scenarios.matters: The hardest part of this incident was not the fix. It was proving to the business that nothing had gone wrong commercially.

scenarios.title: Forty-five days before anyone noticed
scenarios.what: a fare component was missing from 10% of sessions across major US cities for 45 days before detection; automated drift detection cut time-to-detect from ~45 days to about 2
scenarios.situation: A column is fine on average and broken for one city. Your aggregate dashboards are all green.
scenarios.given: 120 days of synthetic daily partitions with per-city breakdown, and a defect injected in one city partway through.
done: Per-segment daily statistics computed (null rate, P50, distinct count)
A forecast-based detector that fires on the anomaly
Measured time-to-detect in days
scenarios.verify: Hidden run injects the defect on a different city and day; harness asserts detection within 3 days.
scenarios.matters: Uber's earlier approach was static thresholds. On trending seasonal data they broke constantly, and people stopped reading the alerts.

scenarios.title: The detector nobody reads
scenarios.what: rule-based per-metric thresholds generated so much noise that investigation became untenable; the fix was aggregating to one table-level score
scenarios.situation: Your monitoring fires 340 alerts a day. It is technically correct. Nobody has looked at it in a month.
scenarios.given: 200 days of per-column daily statistics for a 20-column table, and an existing per-metric alerting rule set.
done: Alert volume measured for the current rules
A table-level score replacing per-metric alerts (PCA or equivalent)
Alert volume and detection recall both reported after the change
scenarios.verify: Harness injects three real defects and asserts your table-level detector catches them at materially lower alert volume.
scenarios.matters: A technically correct detector with bad alert ergonomics is a failed detector. Uber's redesign is a concession to that.

scenarios.title: The bad data was already in the model
scenarios.what: Unity ingested bad data from a large customer, it was baked into the trained model, and the company put the business impact at approximately $110 million for 2022
scenarios.situation: One upstream source has been sending corrupted rows for three weeks. You have already retrained twice. Deleting the rows does not undelete the model.
scenarios.given: A trained classifier, its training set, and one source whose rows have a shifted label distribution.
done: The poisoned source identified from the data alone
Offline accuracy measured on the poisoned holdout and on a clean holdout
A written explanation of why the offline number looked fine
scenarios.verify: Harness retrains from your cleaned set and asserts recovery on the clean holdout.
scenarios.matters: The failure was detected commercially, not technically. By then the corruption was in the weights, and rows could not be un-learned.

scenarios.title: Rows scanned is the only number that matters
scenarios.what: 50+ TB of logs a day, 12,000 queries a day; self-hosted Elasticsearch and an S3+Spark+Trino migration were both abandoned before ClickHouse hit a P99 of 10 seconds
scenarios.situation: The same query takes 40 seconds or 0.4 seconds depending on something you have not looked at yet.
scenarios.given: 5 million synthetic log rows in DuckDB or clickhouse-local, and six queries of varying selectivity.
done: Rows scanned measured for each query
A partitioning or index change applied
Before/after rows scanned and wall-clock for all six
scenarios.verify: Harness runs hidden queries and asserts rows-scanned dropped without result changes.
scenarios.matters: Zomato reported a potential saving of more than USD 1 million. The decision variable throughout was rows scanned.

scenarios.title: A check that writes itself
scenarios.what: Amazon's constraint-suggestion engine produced two wrong constraints on a real dataset — an over-narrow range check and a spurious rule — which is why suggestions need human review
scenarios.situation: Writing validation by hand for every table does not scale; LinkedIn's ad-hoc approach left most datasets unchecked. Generate the checks instead — then find out where generation gets it wrong.
scenarios.given: A 10,000-row dataset in DuckDB, a YAML check schema, and a defect injector.
done: A YAML-to-SQL check generator covering nulls, ranges, uniqueness and distribution
Constraint suggestion from data profiling
At least two suggested constraints that are wrong, identified and explained
The injected defect caught
scenarios.verify: Hidden defects of three classes; harness asserts detection and asserts you documented at least two false suggestions.
scenarios.matters: The paper is unusually honest about its own failures. A suggestion engine you trust blindly will write you a rule that fails every Tuesday.

scenarios.title: Measure the cost before you design the warehouse
scenarios.what: a dedicated warehouse per team was abandoned after they measured 20–40% additional compute cost coming purely from cold starts — found only because query tagging for cost attribution was added first
scenarios.situation: You are asked to pick a warehouse topology. Two designs look equivalent on paper. One of them is 30% more expensive and you cannot tell which without instrumenting first.
scenarios.given: dbt-core with dbt-duckdb, 20 models with refs, and a simulated cold-start cost model.
done: 20 dbt models with refs, tests and a manifest-driven DAG
Query tagging and cost attribution added BEFORE the topology change
Both topologies measured, with the cold-start cost isolated
A recommendation supported by your own numbers
scenarios.verify: Harness parses manifest.json to verify DAG generation and asserts cost attribution exists per model.
scenarios.matters: Instacart only found the 20–40% because they had instrumented cost first. The order of operations is the lesson.

scenarios.title: Beat the neural net with a tuned baseline
scenarios.what: of 18 neural recommenders from top-tier conferences only 7 could be reproduced, and 6 of those 7 were often beaten by properly tuned simple heuristic baselines
scenarios.situation: A paper reports a new architecture beating the state of the art by 12%. You have the same dataset and two hours. Tune the boring baseline properly.
scenarios.given: MovieLens-100k, an item-kNN implementation, and an undertuned neural recommender.
done: The kNN baseline properly tuned with a documented search
Both models evaluated on the same split
A statement of whether the reported gain survives
scenarios.verify: Harness re-runs both on a hidden split and asserts your tuning procedure is reproducible from your config.
scenarios.matters: Once a weak baseline is published it becomes the baseline for the next paper. The error compounds all the way into your production stack.

scenarios.title: The label was the bias
scenarios.org: Optum, studied by Obermeyer et al.
scenarios.what: a widely used care-management algorithm was biased because it predicted healthcare cost as a proxy for illness; race was never an input, and correcting the label would have raised Black patients receiving additional help from 17.7% to 46.5%
scenarios.situation: You have a model with no protected attributes, good accuracy, and a serious fairness problem. The features are fine. Look at what you are predicting.
scenarios.given: A dataset where an observed proxy (spend) is a group-biased measurement of a latent target (need).
done: The model trained on the proxy, evaluated against the latent truth
Disparity quantified at matched risk scores
The same model retrained on a corrected label, with the disparity re-measured
scenarios.verify: Harness recomputes the disparity metric from your predictions on a hidden split.
scenarios.matters: No fairness metric computed against the cost label could ever have surfaced this. The bug was upstream of every metric anyone was watching.

scenarios.title: Where the boosting stops paying
scenarios.what: almost all normalized-entropy improvement came from the first 500 trees; the last 1,000 bought under 0.1%, and on a smaller submodel accuracy actually regressed past 1,000 trees
scenarios.situation: Your GBM improves every time you add trees. Your training time also grows every time you add trees. Find where the trade stops being worth it.
scenarios.given: A 50k-row slice of public CTR data and a gradient boosting implementation.
done: A tree-count sweep with the metric plotted
The saturation point identified with a number
Evidence of overfitting on a deliberately smaller training subset
scenarios.verify: Harness re-runs your sweep config on a hidden slice and asserts the reported saturation point is reproducible.
scenarios.matters: Meta published the exact shape of this curve. Most teams never plot it and pay for the last 1,000 trees forever.

scenarios.title: The embedding that could not have worked
scenarios.what: listing-ID embeddings gave big training-NDCG gains and none on test — a listing can be booked at most 365 times a year, so per-item data is far too sparse for the obvious approach
scenarios.situation: You add per-item ID embeddings because every recommender paper does. Training NDCG jumps. Test NDCG does not move. The cause is not your code.
scenarios.given: A tabular ranking dataset with a high-cardinality item ID and a per-item interaction count distribution.
done: Train and test NDCG both plotted against training steps
The divergence demonstrated
The per-item data volume computed, and the conclusion drawn from it
scenarios.verify: Harness asserts you reported per-item interaction counts alongside the divergence.
scenarios.matters: Airbnb calls this section 'Failed Models'. The root cause is physics, not modelling — no architecture fixes 365 observations a year.

scenarios.title: Accuracy 99.9%, model useless
scenarios.what: card fraud is roughly 0.1% of transactions and decisions must be made inside the authorization path, so the model is tuned against a fixed false-positive budget rather than accuracy
scenarios.situation: Your fraud model is 99.9% accurate. So is a model that predicts 'not fraud' every time. Pick the metric that distinguishes them.
scenarios.given: 10,000 transactions with 0.1% positives.
done: A trivial always-negative baseline scored on accuracy
Precision, recall and PR-AUC reported for both models
An operating point chosen against a stated false-positive budget
scenarios.verify: Harness recomputes metrics at your chosen threshold on a hidden split.
scenarios.matters: The metric that made Radar shippable was recall at a fixed 0.1% false-positive rate. Accuracy never entered the decision.

scenarios.title: The feature importances that changed their mind
scenarios.what: JVM XGBoost 0.81 and earlier computed unreliable feature importances, which teams had been using to make feature-selection decisions
scenarios.situation: You drop the five least important features and your model gets better. You re-run the importance calculation with a different seed and the bottom five are different features.
scenarios.given: A tabular dataset with correlated features and a boosting implementation.
done: Feature importances computed across several seeds and methods
The instability quantified
A more defensible selection procedure applied, with its result
scenarios.verify: Harness re-runs your selection procedure and asserts it produces a stable feature set across seeds.
scenarios.matters: Uber's teams were making real production decisions on numbers that were quietly wrong. The fix is not a better number — it is a procedure that survives re-running.

scenarios.title: 'Reported' is not 'fraud'
scenarios.what: users could report a transaction as suspicious with one tap, so a large slice of positives were ordinary commercial disputes; training on raw reports poisoned the model until a segmentation step stripped high-false-positive cohorts
scenarios.situation: You have 50,000 UPI transactions and a label column called `reported`. Everyone on the team is treating it as ground truth. It is not.
scenarios.given: 50,000 transactions with a noisy `reported` label, cohort attributes, and a small clean-labelled holdout.
done: A model trained on the raw label, scored on the clean holdout
Cohort analysis identifying the high-false-positive segments
A cleaned training set with those cohorts handled, and the improvement measured
Extreme class imbalance handled with an explicit operating point
scenarios.verify: Hidden clean holdout; harness asserts improvement comes from label treatment and not from threshold tuning alone.
scenarios.matters: PhonePe reported a 40% reduction in consumer fraud rate. The unlock was recognising the label meant something different from what it was named.

scenarios.title: Trees that make features for a linear model
scenarios.what: leaf-index features from boosted trees fed into a linear model reduced normalized entropy by more than 3.4% relative — against a background where feature engineering typically moves it by a fraction of a percent
scenarios.situation: Two model families, each fine on its own. The published result says composing them beats both by a margin that dwarfs anything else in the paper.
scenarios.given: A 50k-row CTR slice, a GBM, and a logistic regression.
done: GBM and LR baselines each measured
Leaf indices extracted, one-hot encoded, fed to LR
Normalized entropy reported for all three
A per-weight learning-rate comparison showing why the global rate fails
scenarios.verify: Harness re-fits your pipeline on a hidden slice and asserts the composed model beats both baselines.
scenarios.matters: This is a decade-old paper that still beats most first attempts at tabular CTR, and it costs nothing to run on a laptop.

scenarios.title: The long tail nobody has data for
scenarios.what: restricting real-time scoring to the ~1% of items that actually need it cut computation cost by approximately 80%
scenarios.situation: Five thousand items, ninety days of observations, and most items have fewer than five data points. Scoring all of them in real time is affordable at your scale and would not be at Instacart's.
scenarios.given: 5,000 items × 90 days of availability observations with a deliberately long tail.
done: A long-window frequency component and a short-window signal component built separately
A rule identifying which items actually need real-time scoring
Cost measured for score-everything vs score-the-1%
Accuracy compared for both, especially on the tail
scenarios.verify: Hidden item set weighted toward the tail; harness asserts the selective strategy holds accuracy while cutting compute.
scenarios.matters: The prior batch system was stale and expensive at once. Both problems had the same fix, and it was a routing decision rather than a modelling one.

scenarios.title: Train before the shift, act after it
scenarios.what: Zillow's Q3 2021 results included a ~$304 million inventory write-down because homes were bought above the company's own subsequent estimate of resale value; Zillow Offers was wound down and about 25% of staff were laid off
scenarios.situation: You have a price model with respectable error on its test set. A business rule turns each prediction into an irreversible purchase. Then the market moves. Show what happens to the balance sheet, not to the RMSE.
scenarios.given: A public house-price dataset spanning a regime change, and a buy-rule specification with a margin parameter.
done: A model trained strictly on the pre-shift period
Error measured on pre-shift and post-shift holdouts separately
A simulated buy rule acting on point predictions, with cumulative capital position tracked
The error distribution — not just the mean — modelled and shown to widen
A monitoring design that would have halted purchasing, with the trigger it fires on
A written recommendation on what margin the business should have required
scenarios.verify: Hidden post-shift period; harness asserts your monitor fires before cumulative loss exceeds a stated threshold.
scenarios.matters: The point predictions were not really the problem. Zillow scaled volume as if forecast error were stable, and the error band widened while the business had no hedge.

scenarios.title: AUC 0.83 or 0.63, depending on when you look
scenarios.what: external validation found AUC 0.63 against the vendor's 0.76–0.83; recomputing AUC to include scores up to 3 hours AFTER sepsis onset reproduced the vendor's number at 0.80
scenarios.situation: The same model, the same data, two AUC numbers 0.20 apart. The difference is entirely in when you allow the prediction to count.
scenarios.given: A 10,000-row time-stamped patient event table with onset times.
done: The model scored with a strictly pre-onset prediction window
The model scored again including post-onset predictions
Both AUCs reported, and the gap explained in one paragraph
scenarios.verify: Harness recomputes both windows from your prediction file and asserts the gap is present and correctly attributed.
scenarios.matters: This model was live at hundreds of hospitals before anyone outside the vendor checked. The flaw was in the evaluation, not the model.

scenarios.title: Thirty-three percent sensitivity at the shipping threshold
scenarios.what: at the recommended threshold: sensitivity 33%, positive predictive value 12%, on a 6.6% sepsis incidence — the model missed 1,709 of 2,552 cases
scenarios.situation: Your AUC is defensible. Now compute what a clinician actually experiences at the threshold you plan to ship.
scenarios.given: An imbalanced tabular dataset at ~6% positive rate and a trained model.
done: AUC reported
Sensitivity, specificity and PPV computed at the intended operating threshold
Alerts per 1,000 patients and false alerts per true positive
A one-line verdict on whether the business case survives
scenarios.verify: Harness recomputes all operating-point metrics from your predictions and threshold.
scenarios.matters: AUC 0.63 is a bad number. The number that mattered was that clinicians got eight false alerts for every real one.

scenarios.title: The model learned which hospital took the photo
scenarios.what: of 2,212 studies reviewed, none of the 61 models assessed in depth were judged of potential clinical use — with 'Frankenstein datasets' and duplicate images across splits among the named failures
scenarios.situation: You will build a classifier with near-perfect accuracy in twenty minutes. It will be worthless, and you will prove it yourself.
scenarios.given: Two small public image sets from different sources, plus a mixed-source holdout.

Near-perfect accuracy on the naive split demonstrated
Accuracy on a mixed-source holdout demonstrated to collapse
The mechanism named in one sentence
scenarios.verify: Harness evaluates your model on a hidden mixed-source set and asserts the collapse.
scenarios.matters: Hundreds of teams published this exact mistake during 2020 with near-perfect reported accuracy. It takes twenty minutes to reproduce and you never forget it.

scenarios.title: The surrogate metric with a false constant
scenarios.what: an Office Online team used clicks × an assumed constant conversion rate as a revenue surrogate; treatment showed a 64% reduction in clicks, but the constant assumption was false and the read was wrong
scenarios.situation: Your A/B test shows the treatment is catastrophically worse on your surrogate metric. The surrogate contains an assumption nobody has checked since it was written.
scenarios.given: A simulated experiment log with a surrogate metric whose conversion assumption breaks in the treatment arm.
done: The apparent regression reproduced
The broken assumption located
The corrected read, with the direction of the true effect stated
scenarios.verify: Harness re-runs with a different injected assumption break and asserts you locate it.
scenarios.matters: Microsoft's paper is a catalogue of results that were wrong on first read. Every one of them passed a significance test.

scenarios.title: Every gate was green
scenarios.what: offline evals 'generally looked good' and the A/B test showed users preferred the new model — because sycophancy is exactly what short-horizon preference metrics reward; it was rolled back within about four days
scenarios.situation: Your evaluation set has a blind spot. A change that scores higher on every metric you have is obviously worse on a dimension you never wrote down.
scenarios.given: A 30-prompt eval set with a deliberate blind spot, and two model variants.
done: Variant B shown to score higher on the existing eval
Variant B shown to be worse on a held-out dimension you define
Three eval items added that would have caught it
scenarios.verify: Hidden eval items test whether your additions generalise beyond the specific failure shown.
scenarios.matters: The most valuable line in OpenAI's postmortem is that expert testers said it felt off before launch, and the green dashboard won.

scenarios.title: Better offline, no better business
scenarios.what: across 23 comparisons where a new model beat the old one offline, the correlation between offline gain and business-metric gain was Pearson −0.1 (90% CI −0.45 to 0.27)
scenarios.situation: Eight model variants, cleanly ranked by AUC. You are about to ship the top one. Simulate what it does to the business metric first.
scenarios.given: A 10k-row click/conversion dataset and a business-value function with a deliberately non-monotone relationship to model score.
done: 8 model variants trained and ranked by offline metric
A simulated business metric computed for each
The correlation between the two rankings reported
At least one of the four Booking mechanisms (saturation, segment saturation, uncanny valley, over-optimisation) demonstrated
scenarios.verify: Harness recomputes the rank correlation from your results and asserts you named the mechanism you demonstrated.
scenarios.matters: Booking had roughly 150 models in production and enough discipline to publish a negative result about all of them. Most teams never measure this at all.

scenarios.title: The features were older in production
scenarios.what: offline and online AUC diverged, traced to feature staleness (the online pipeline lagged 1–2 days) and cached residuals (uploads added keys without evicting stale ones)
scenarios.situation: Offline AUC says +2%. Online AUC says nothing changed. Both numbers are correct.
scenarios.given: A feature table with timestamps, a training pipeline, and a simulated online store with a configurable lag and a cache that never evicts.
done: A point-in-time-correct training set built
The skew reproduced by serving with lagged features
The stale-cache failure reproduced separately
Both effects quantified independently
scenarios.verify: Harness serves a hidden request set through your pipeline and asserts your reported skew matches the measured one.
scenarios.matters: Two separate mechanisms produced the same symptom. Teams that fix one and declare victory get to find the other in a month.

scenarios.title: The reward distribution moved under you
scenarios.what: off-the-shelf contextual bandits struggled in an environment where reward distributions shift match-to-match; the deployed hierarchical policy showed a 0.4% revenue improvement in A/B, then a further 0.5%
scenarios.situation: Your bandit converges beautifully. Then the context changes — an IPL final does not behave like a Tuesday league game — and yesterday's optimal arm is today's worst.
scenarios.given: A non-stationary bandit simulator with reward distributions that shift every N rounds.
done: A flat contextual bandit and a fixed policy both implemented as baselines
A hierarchical or adaptive variant implemented
Cumulative regret plotted for all three across shifts
Cold-start behaviour on a new context measured
scenarios.verify: Hidden shift schedule; harness asserts your adaptive policy beats both baselines on cumulative regret.
scenarios.matters: Dream11's gains are fractions of a percent. At their volume that is the entire business case, and it only exists because the policy adapts.

scenarios.title: The evaluation harness you commit before the model
scenarios.what: every evaluation failure in this unit shares one property: the threshold, the window or the metric was decided after seeing results
scenarios.situation: You are handed a problem, a dataset and no model. Before you train anything, ship the harness that will decide whether the model is good — including the thresholds, the splits, and the questions it must not get wrong.
scenarios.given: A tabular dataset with a temporal dimension and a known-but-undisclosed leakage vector.
done: A preregistered evaluation plan committed before any model code
Temporally correct splits with the leakage vector defended against
Operating-point metrics, not just ranking metrics, with thresholds fixed in advance
A deliberate blind-spot audit: three ways this eval could pass a bad model
A simulated business-value function and the offline/online correlation reported
Results reported honestly, including where your own model fails
scenarios.verify: Harness verifies the eval plan predates model commits by git timestamp, replays your splits for leakage, and scores your model on a hidden set at your preregistered threshold.
scenarios.matters: This is the artifact that separates the U5 unit from a Kaggle notebook. Fixing thresholds after seeing results is the single most common way teams fool themselves.

scenarios.title: The network that would not learn until you scaled the inputs
scenarios.what: Airbnb's neural ranking work documents feature normalisation as a concrete failure and fix — unnormalised features left the network in a plateau
scenarios.situation: Your loss plateaus immediately and stays there. The architecture is fine. Look at the input distributions.
scenarios.given: A tabular dataset with features on wildly different scales, and a small MLP.
done: The plateau reproduced with raw features
Feature distributions plotted before and after transformation
The paper's transforms applied and the loss curve compared
scenarios.verify: Harness trains your config on a hidden split and asserts convergence.
scenarios.matters: It is the most boring bug in deep learning and it cost a very good team real time. Plot your inputs first.

scenarios.title: Twenty-one percent of usable images, rejected
scenarios.what: a model trained on high-quality scans shipped with a hard gradability gate; in real clinics with poor lighting, more than a fifth of captured images were auto-rejected despite nurses judging them readable, with no override path
scenarios.situation: Your model has a quality gate. It was calibrated on clean data. Your users work in a room with bad lighting and a queue outside the door.
scenarios.given: A small image classifier, a clean test set, and the same images degraded (blur, low light, JPEG artefacts, off-centre crop).
done: Rejection rate measured on clean and degraded inputs
Accuracy measured on the images the gate would have rejected
A recommendation on the gate, including whether a human override should exist
scenarios.verify: Harness runs a hidden degraded set and asserts you reported accuracy on rejected-but-usable inputs.
scenarios.matters: The model exported its training distribution as an operating requirement onto rooms that could not meet it. Nurses started editing images to get them accepted.

scenarios.title: Your laptop is the median device
scenarios.what: on the real Android fleet the median GPU is no faster than the CPU, the compute DSP exists on about 5% of targeted SoCs, and 72% of primary CPU cores in use were designed years earlier
scenarios.situation: The deployment plan says 'run it on the GPU'. Most of your users do not have a useful one. Benchmark honestly on the hardware you actually have.
scenarios.given: MobileNetV2 or a small CNN, and a quantisation toolchain.
done: Float32 inference latency measured on CPU
Int8 quantised latency and accuracy measured
The accuracy cost of quantisation reported alongside the speedup
A deployment recommendation for a low-end device fleet
scenarios.verify: Harness re-runs your benchmark script and asserts both latency and accuracy are reported for both precisions.
scenarios.matters: The constraint that makes this scenario awkward on an 8 GB laptop is exactly the constraint Meta is describing. You are the low-end device.

scenarios.title: The sophisticated option that lost
scenarios.what: GradNorm adaptive loss weighting — the obvious sophisticated choice — lost to simpler weighting; and converting embeddings to binary caused a significant accuracy drop under the baseline normalisation setup
scenarios.situation: You have a multi-task model and two ways to weight the losses: an adaptive method with a paper behind it, and a constant you picked in five minutes. Measure both.
scenarios.given: Three small embedding heads on three small image sets, with a shared backbone.
done: Both weighting schemes trained and evaluated per task
The comparison reported per task, not averaged
A float-to-binary embedding conversion with the accuracy cost measured
scenarios.verify: Harness re-runs both configs on a hidden task split.
scenarios.matters: Pinterest published both dead ends. The adaptive method is more interesting to read about and lost on their data.

scenarios.title: Three models in one step
scenarios.what: packing several models into a single dense processing step created accelerator-memory pressure; median preview latency fell from 111.7 minutes to 3.7 after the pipeline was restructured
scenarios.situation: Your pipeline loads three models into one processing step and falls over. Splitting them costs you a serialisation boundary. Measure which is worse.
scenarios.given: A local Beam DirectRunner pipeline with three small models and 500 elements.
done: Per-element latency and peak memory measured with all three models in one step
The same measured with the models split across steps
A recommendation with both numbers stated
scenarios.verify: Harness runs both topologies on a hidden element set and asserts memory was actually measured, not estimated.
scenarios.matters: The 30x improvement was a topology change, not a model change. It is the sort of win that never shows up in a model card.

scenarios.title: Wake word, two thresholds
scenarios.what: early iterations trained on utterances captured after a button press — the wrong acoustic conditions for far-field activation; the shipped design used a small always-on detector cascading to a larger one, with a dual-threshold 'second chance'
scenarios.situation: An always-on detector must run continuously on a battery and almost never fire by accident. You cannot have both accuracy and cheapness in one model, so build two.
scenarios.given: The free Google Speech Commands dataset, CPU-trainable in minutes.
done: A small first-stage detector and a larger second-stage detector
The cascade wired with two thresholds
FAR/FRR curves plotted for the small model, the large model and the cascade
Compute cost per hour of audio measured for each
scenarios.verify: Hidden audio set including deliberately near-miss utterances; harness asserts the cascade's cost/accuracy point dominates either model alone.
scenarios.matters: Apple's training-data mismatch is the reusable lesson: data collected under the wrong conditions is worse than less data collected under the right ones.

scenarios.title: Five thousand categories, most of them nearly empty
scenarios.what: classification into a 7-level, 5,500-category taxonomy where class imbalance was the main modelling obstacle; the multimodal model raised precision by eight percent while coverage almost doubled
scenarios.situation: Classify products into a deep taxonomy where the head categories have thousands of examples and the tail has three.
scenarios.given: A few thousand product records with a short text field and a thumbnail, over a hierarchical taxonomy.
done: A text-only baseline and an image+text model both built with frozen pretrained encoders
Precision and coverage reported for both
Head and tail performance reported separately
Class imbalance handled explicitly, with the method stated
scenarios.verify: Hidden tail-weighted test set; harness asserts head/tail results are reported separately.
scenarios.matters: The averaged number hides the taxonomy. A model that is excellent on the head and useless on the tail reads as 'good' until a merchant lists something unusual.

scenarios.title: Ten megabytes, in a cotton field, offline
scenarios.what: pest-counting for Indian smallholder cotton farmers, where trap photos vary wildly by phone, light and angle, ground truth is hard to obtain, and conventional ML metrics did not map onto the agricultural decision that mattered
scenarios.situation: Ship an image model that runs on a cheap Android phone with no connectivity, on photos taken by people who are not photographers, where the output is not a class label but an action recommendation.
scenarios.given: A few thousand images of small objects on textured backgrounds, with counts, deliberately varied in lighting and angle.
done: A counting model trained on CPU
Pruned and quantised to under 10 MB, with the accuracy cost measured at each step
Robustness measured across lighting and angle variation
A decision layer mapping counts to a recommended action, with its own threshold
Evaluation against the decision, not just against the count
An offline inference path with no network dependency
scenarios.verify: Hidden image set from unseen conditions; harness asserts model size is under 10 MB and that decision-level accuracy is reported alongside count accuracy.
scenarios.matters: The paper's honesty is the point: conventional metrics did not map to the agricultural decision. A model that counts well and advises badly has failed.

scenarios.title: Fine at K=100, broken at K=1000
scenarios.what: HNSW lost about 5% recall at K=100 but blew past 10% loss at K=1000, which was the regime Etsy actually retrieved in; they switched to a 4-bit product-quantiser index with 5x over-fetch and re-ranking
scenarios.situation: Your ANN index benchmarks beautifully. Your benchmark uses K=10. Production retrieves a thousand candidates.
scenarios.given: 150,000 vectors from a free sentence-transformer, an exact baseline, and an HNSW index.
done: Recall measured against exact search at K=10, 100 and 1000
The degradation curve plotted
An over-fetch-and-rerank strategy applied, with recall and latency after
scenarios.verify: Harness re-runs your config on a hidden query set at all three K values.
scenarios.matters: The index was never wrong. The benchmark was measuring a regime the product does not operate in.

scenarios.title: Milliseconds to seconds, then a circuit breaker
scenarios.what: when the KNN graph was not given enough allocated memory, query time degraded from milliseconds to tens of seconds because of disk I/O, and the memory circuit breaker produced collapse rather than graceful degradation
scenarios.situation: Your index fits in RAM on your machine. Constrain the memory and watch the failure mode — it is not a gentle slowdown.
scenarios.given: A vector index sized to sit just under your available RAM, and a memory limiter.
done: Query latency measured with the index resident
Latency measured with memory constrained below index size
The failure characterised: is it degradation or collapse?
A sizing rule derived from your measurements
scenarios.verify: Harness runs your sizing rule against a hidden index size and asserts it predicts the cliff.
scenarios.matters: This is easier to demonstrate on a small laptop than on a big server, which makes it one of the rare cases where the 8 GB constraint is an advantage.

scenarios.title: Better data beat a better model by 5x
scenarios.what: upgrading the embedding model on raw metadata gave +5.92% Hit@5; rewriting the input representation gave +31.22%, and stacking the model upgrade on top added only about 6 more points
scenarios.situation: You can spend your week upgrading the embedding model or cleaning the text you feed it. The published answer is a controlled 2×2 and it is not close.
scenarios.given: 5,000 listings with messy real text, two embedding models, and a rewriting step.
done: All four arms of the 2×2 run (raw/clean × model A/model B)
Hit@5 reported for each arm
The larger lever identified with numbers
scenarios.verify: Harness re-runs all four arms on a hidden query set.
scenarios.matters: This is the single most useful ablation in the unit because it is cheap, it is decisive, and it contradicts where most teams put their week.

scenarios.title: Semantic search that cannot find an exact term
scenarios.what: dense retrieval often failed to match traditional IR on exact term matching and cost more per query, which forced it to ship as an additional retrieval source blended with Elasticsearch rather than a replacement
scenarios.situation: Your semantic search is better on paraphrase and worse on exact names. Build the eval set that shows both, before someone in product finds out the hard way.
scenarios.given: A 20,000-document corpus, BM25, and a sentence-transformer.
done: An adversarial eval set with paraphrase queries AND exact-term queries
Both retrievers scored on both query classes
A recommendation on replace-vs-blend supported by the split results
scenarios.verify: Hidden queries in both classes; harness asserts you reported results split by query class.
scenarios.matters: The averaged number said dense retrieval was better. The split number said replacing lexical search would break every query containing a proper noun.

scenarios.title: Popular because the vector is bigger
scenarios.what: roughly 2 million new items a day for 180M+ users; embedding norm growth is entangled with popularity, so a recommender can amplify already-popular content simply because those embeddings have larger norms
scenarios.situation: Fresh items have unreliable embeddings and popular items have large ones. Your similarity search is quietly a popularity ranker.
scenarios.given: MovieLens-25M or a slice, with incremental embedding training and interaction counts.
done: L2 norm plotted against interaction count
Cosine drift from the final embedding plotted against interaction count
A maturity threshold derived from your own curves
Retrieval results compared with and without immature items filtered
scenarios.verify: Harness recomputes norm/count correlation from your snapshots.
scenarios.matters: Two million new items a day means most of your catalogue is always immature. The bias is structural, not incidental.

scenarios.title: Blend, don't replace
scenarios.what: Spotify shipped dense retrieval as an additional source blended with Elasticsearch, because it could not match lexical search on exact terms and cost more per query
scenarios.situation: Build the hybrid your U7-M04 results argued for, and prove the blend beats either component on the combined query set.
scenarios.given: The same 20,000-document corpus, BM25, a sentence-transformer, and a query set spanning both classes.
done: BM25 and dense retrieval both working independently
A fusion strategy implemented (RRF or weighted score normalisation)
Recall and MRR reported for BM25, dense and hybrid separately
Per-query-class results showing the blend does not regress either class
Latency and per-query cost measured for all three
scenarios.verify: Hidden query set in both classes; harness asserts hybrid does not regress either class relative to the better single retriever.
scenarios.matters: The fusion is ten lines. The discipline is refusing to accept an average that hides a regression on one query class.

scenarios.title: Stage one alone makes it worse
scenarios.what: unsupervised domain adaptation alone improved Precision@1 but LOWERED overall MAP; supervised fine-tuning without domain adaptation also performed worse; only the two stages together won
scenarios.situation: A two-stage training recipe where either stage on its own makes the system worse than doing nothing. Most teams stop after stage one because Precision@1 goes up.
scenarios.given: A 10,000-item food catalogue spanning multiple regional cuisines, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, and a labelled relevance set.
done: Baseline, stage-1-only, stage-2-only and both-stages all evaluated
MAP and Precision@1 both reported for all four
The stage-1-only trap demonstrated with numbers
CPU query-encode latency measured against a 100ms budget
scenarios.verify: Hidden relevance set spanning cuisines; harness asserts all four arms were run and both metrics reported.
scenarios.matters: Precision@1 went up and MAP went down. A team watching one metric ships the worse system and believes they improved it.

scenarios.title: Asking it whether it was lying
scenarios.what: an attorney filed six fabricated cases; when opposing counsel could not find them he asked ChatGPT whether they were real, it said yes, and he swore an affidavit on that basis — $5,000 in Rule 11 sanctions followed
scenarios.situation: Ask a model for citations in a niche domain. Then ask it to verify its own citations. Then check them against a real index.
scenarios.given: A free-tier model and access to a real reference index (CourtListener, Crossref or PubMed).
done: 20 citations generated in a niche domain
The model's own self-verification result recorded for each
A deterministic existence check against a real index
Fabrication rate reported, and self-verification accuracy reported separately
scenarios.verify: Harness re-runs your existence checker against a known set of real and fake identifiers.
scenarios.matters: The verification loop was closed inside the system that produced the error. That is the whole lesson and it costs nothing to reproduce.

scenarios.title: Ten percent malformed, and re-prompting was the wrong fix
scenarios.what: roughly 10% of structured outputs were syntactically or schema-wise invalid; re-prompting cost unacceptable latency, so they wrote a defensive parser and took errors to ~0.01%
scenarios.situation: One call in ten comes back malformed. The obvious fix is to ask again. Measure what asking again costs you.
scenarios.given: A 4–5 field typed schema and a free-tier model.
done: 300 calls run and every parse failure logged by class
Failure classes counted (invalid syntax, missing field, wrong type, extra field)
Re-prompting implemented and its added latency measured
A defensive parser implemented and its residual error rate measured
scenarios.verify: Hidden prompt set; harness asserts both strategies were measured on latency and residual error.
scenarios.matters: This is the most honest structured-output report any large company has published, and the counter-intuitive part is that the fix is a parser, not a prompt.

scenarios.title: One prompt doing three jobs badly
scenarios.what: a single generic rewrite prompt produced valid but useless output ('1% milk' → 'one percent milk') and covered only about half of search traffic; decomposing into three task-specific prompts fixed it
scenarios.situation: Your rewrite prompt produces output that passes every validity check and helps nobody.
scenarios.given: 300 real-shaped search queries and a free-tier model.
done: Arm A: one generic rewrite prompt
Arm B: three task-specific prompts with distinct objectives
Useful-rewrite rate measured for both, with 'useful' defined in advance
Coverage of the query set reported for both
scenarios.verify: Hidden query set; harness asserts your usefulness criterion was defined before the arms were run.
scenarios.matters: Valid and useless is the hardest failure mode to catch, because every automated check passes.

scenarios.title: Precompute the head of the distribution
scenarios.what: up to 100x cost savings versus calling a complex frontier prompt directly, achieved by using a fine-tuned small model for offline precomputation of the head of the query distribution
scenarios.situation: Your query log is Zipf-distributed. A small fraction of distinct queries covers most of your traffic. You are paying frontier prices for all of it.
scenarios.given: A 10,000-query log with a realistic long tail, and two model tiers.
done: The head/tail split measured (what % of traffic is covered by what % of distinct queries)
A precompute-the-head, live-serve-the-tail strategy implemented
Total cost measured before and after
Quality on head and tail reported separately
scenarios.verify: Harness replays a hidden query log through your router and recomputes cost and coverage.
scenarios.matters: This is the cheapest large cost win in the entire curriculum and it requires no model change whatsoever.

scenarios.title: Three times the tokens for the same sentence
scenarios.what: Indic languages are roughly 1% of Common Crawl while India is about 18% of world population; general-purpose tokenizers handle Indic scripts inefficiently and code-mixing poorly
scenarios.situation: The same meaning costs you three times as many tokens in Hindi as in English. That is a latency bill, a cost bill and a context-window bill at once.
scenarios.given: 200 parallel sentences in English, Hindi, Tamil and Bengali, plus code-mixed examples, and several tokenizers.
done: Tokens-per-sentence measured per language per tokenizer
Fertility ratio computed against English
Cost and context-window impact projected for a realistic workload
Code-mixed behaviour examined separately
scenarios.verify: Harness recomputes fertility from your tokenizer configs on a hidden parallel set.
scenarios.matters: Every Indian-language product pays this tax. Most teams discover it when the context window overflows in production.

scenarios.title: Asking for everything made it worse at everything
scenarios.what: asking the model to predict all fields during fine-tuning led to a loss of generalisability at inference; randomised selective field extraction improved both accuracy and performance
scenarios.situation: Your extraction prompt asks for all 12 fields every time. It scores worse than a prompt asking for three.
scenarios.given: 200 messy product listings and a 12-field schema.
done: All-fields extraction accuracy measured per field
Selective (randomised subset) extraction accuracy measured per field
The comparison reported per field, not averaged
A conclusion on output-shape overfitting
scenarios.verify: Hidden listings and hidden field subsets; harness asserts per-field reporting.
scenarios.matters: The model was overfitting to the shape of the answer rather than to the content. It is invisible unless you vary the shape.

scenarios.title: Route the traffic, learn the prices
scenarios.what: over 25% cost savings with no degradation on a 6-second-deadline reranker; the motivating discovery was that their prior assumptions about tier behaviour were wrong, so any hand-written static routing table was already mispriced
scenarios.situation: Four model endpoints with different cost, latency and failure characteristics. Your static routing table was written from assumptions nobody re-checked.
scenarios.given: Four mock models with configurable cost, log-normal latency distributions that deliberately overlap, and failure rates.
done: A static routing baseline implemented from stated assumptions
Thompson sampling routing implemented
Cost, deadline-hit rate and error rate measured for both
Caller-error traffic excluded from the reward signal, with the reason documented
Behaviour shown when a provider's latency distribution shifts mid-run
scenarios.verify: Hidden provider configuration with a mid-run shift; harness asserts the adaptive router adapts and the static one does not.
scenarios.matters: The static table is not wrong because it is static. It is wrong because it encodes assumptions that were never measured.

scenarios.title: Two hundred columns will not fit
scenarios.what: tables with 200+ columns consumed 40–60K tokens of schema alone and broke calls against a 32K context limit; accuracy also declined as more tables were onboarded because plain similarity search returned irrelevant schemas
scenarios.situation: Natural language to SQL over 40 tables. Several are 200 columns wide. Several have confusingly similar names. Your first version worked on seven tables and got worse as you added more.
scenarios.given: A SQLite warehouse with 40 tables including deliberately wide and confusingly-named ones, plus 40 questions with gold SQL.
done: Arm A: all schemas in one prompt — the context overflow demonstrated
Arm B: a schema selection or decomposition step before generation
Exact-result-match accuracy for both arms
Accuracy plotted as table count grows from 7 to 40
Token count per request measured for both
scenarios.verify: Hidden question set over the same warehouse; harness asserts the accuracy-vs-table-count curve was measured.
scenarios.matters: The naive version degraded as it succeeded. That is the shape of the problem — it works in the demo and fails as adoption grows.

scenarios.title: The table that got shredded
scenarios.what: off-the-shelf PDF loaders destroyed tables spanning 5+ pages with nested cells — cells became isolated text disconnected from their row and column headers, so semantic search could never find the right value
scenarios.situation: Load a PDF containing a multi-page nested table with a standard loader. Read the output. The numbers are all still there and none of them mean anything.
scenarios.given: 3 real PDFs containing multi-page nested tables, and a standard PDF loader.
done: The shredded output produced and inspected
Five specific questions the shredded text cannot answer, with evidence
A table-aware extraction path that preserves row and column headers
The same five questions answered correctly after
scenarios.verify: Hidden PDF with a different table structure; harness asserts your extraction preserves header association.
scenarios.matters: This is the single highest-value 40 minutes in the RAG unit. Everyone builds RAG over PDFs. Almost nobody looks at what the loader produced.

scenarios.title: Smaller chunks won
scenarios.what: on dense acronym-saturated technical standards, 125-token chunks beat the standard 500-token default — an inverse relationship between chunk size and accuracy, the opposite of the usual prose intuition
scenarios.situation: Every tutorial says 500 tokens with overlap. On your corpus that is the worst setting you could have picked.
scenarios.given: An acronym-heavy technical corpus (RFCs or an API spec) and a 60-question eval set.
done: A chunk-size sweep at 100 / 250 / 500 / 1000 tokens
Retrieval accuracy plotted against chunk size
The best setting identified for THIS corpus
A one-line explanation of why the default is wrong here
scenarios.verify: Hidden question set over the same corpus; harness asserts the sweep covered all four sizes.
scenarios.matters: There is no correct chunk size. There is a correct chunk size for your corpus, and it takes an hour to find.

scenarios.title: It invented a policy to explain a bug
scenarios.what: a race condition was logging users out; asked why, the support AI invented a subscription policy that did not exist, non-deterministically, and users cancelled subscriptions over it
scenarios.situation: Give a model a knowledge base that deliberately does not cover the question being asked, then ask twenty times and count how many different answers you get.
scenarios.given: A 10-document policy KB with a deliberate coverage gap, and a free-tier model.
done: The same uncovered question asked 20 times at non-zero temperature
The distinct answers counted and the invented facts listed
An abstain path added
Abstain rate and false-abstain rate both measured after
scenarios.verify: Hidden uncovered questions; harness asserts abstention fires on gaps without over-firing on covered questions.
scenarios.matters: The bug was a race condition. The damage was the confabulated explanation, and it was different every time it was asked.

scenarios.title: A real citation for a claim it does not support
scenarios.what: audited legal RAG products hallucinated between 17% and 33% of the time despite vendor claims of elimination; the new failure mode is a fluent answer with an authoritative-looking citation that does not support the proposition
scenarios.situation: Every answer has a citation. Every citation is to a real document. Some of those documents do not say what the answer claims.
scenarios.given: A 50-document corpus, a working RAG pipeline, and 30 questions including deliberate false-premise ones.
done: Retrieval failure and grounding failure scored as separate categories
Each answer's citation checked for whether it actually supports the claim
Rates reported for both failure types
False-premise questions handled and scored separately
scenarios.verify: Hidden question set with false premises; harness asserts you scored grounding separately from retrieval.
scenarios.matters: RAG reduces hallucination and does not remove it, and it introduces a failure mode plain LLMs do not have: confident wrongness wearing a citation.

scenarios.title: Chunking destroyed the structure
